column4: what the Report says it is and does
column5: The Berg Report (World Bank, September 1981; African Strategy Review Group led by Elliot Berg with K. Y. Amoako, Rolf Gusten, Jacob Meerman and Gene Tidrick) states that it was requested by the Bank's African Governors in 1979, 'accepts the long-term objectives' of the Lagos Plan, 'builds on' it, and 'offers no general prescriptions' because countries differ. It lists three causes of poor growth: internal 'structural' factors (underdeveloped human resources, disruption of colonisation, climate, rapid population growth), external factors (stagflation, energy prices, slow primary trade, terms of trade), and domestic policy inadequacies (trade and exchange-rate policy that protected industry and held back agriculture; an overextended public sector; a consistent bias against agriculture). The course's table says critics think the Report undervalued external shocks: that is fair as an argument, but the Report does address them (its chapter 3). Present it as a three-part diagnosis with policy emphasised.

The Report recommends a doubling of aid in real terms by the end of the 1980s (from 4.9 to 9.1 billion dollars, or 17.8 billion in current prices), together with policy reform, to reach about 2.5 per cent a year per-capita growth, against zero or negative otherwise; it says donors have 'contributed to the present crisis' and asks for a 'new social compact'. Figures cited: sub-Saharan population 343.9 million (1979); GNP per head 329 dollars excluding Nigeria; life expectancy 47; food production up 1.5 per cent a year in the 1970s against population growth of 2.7 per cent; debt up from 6 to 32 billion dollars 1970 to 1979 and debt service from 6 to 12 per cent of exports; 19 countries with under 1 per cent per-capita growth 1960 to 1979 and 15 with negative growth in the 1970s. It is a pro-aid document: place it beside Moyo (who wants aid cut) and Rodney.

The Report's chapter 2 lists what independence inherited: Zaire left without a single African doctor, lawyer, engineer or army officer; Nigerians held fewer than 700 of 3,000 senior civil service posts until the mid-1950s; 1,500 French technical staff held almost all top jobs in Senegal in 1961; in Kenya and Tanzania fewer than 20 per cent of high-level civil-service posts were in African hands at independence. A World Bank source for the Module 4 'inheritance' figures that agrees with Hochschild and Rodney on the Congo (the figures are the Bank's, tied to manpower surveys of that period).

Chapter 3 says external forces 'were not the chief factor' behind growing deficits: for oil importers poor export performance was more significant than oil prices or terms of trade (export volume fell in two thirds of countries with data in the 1970s), although the second oil shock and the collapse of non-mineral commodity prices hit at the end of the decade. Chapter 4 argues that real official exchange rates became overvalued because home inflation outran inflation abroad, which cut incentives for export crops (examples: cocoa in Ghana, sisal in Tanzania, coffee in Madagascar) and raised food imports, and that marketing boards taxed farmers (the Ghana Cocoa Marketing Board example). So the course's table is right that the Report weighed policy above shocks, and the critics' point about external shocks is a real contrast, but the Report also praises achievements (primary enrolment 36 to 63 per cent, life expectancy 39 to 47) and population growth is treated as a structural constraint.

Berg's PDF text interleaves two columns, so quotations and numbers are hard to match exactly. I read the introduction block in full (chunks 1 to 3) and the first of four chunks of the second block; chunks 2 to 4 of the second block were served but only searched for passages on overvalued exchange rates and marketing boards. The remaining nine blocks (agriculture, human resources, other sectors, longer-term issues, external assistance, statistical annex) were not read.
